Introduction to the Dynamic Nelson-Siegel Model

dnsr package

2026-10-08

Source: vignettes/dns-model-introduction.Rmd
dns-model-introduction.Rmd

Overview

The dnsr package provides a comprehensive implementation of the Dynamic Nelson-Siegel (DNS) model for yield curve modeling and analysis. This vignette introduces the model and demonstrates how to use the package for yield curve fitting, factor dynamics estimation, and scenario simulation.

Note: This vignette covers the basic functionality of the package. For advanced stochastic simulation using the YUIMA package, please see the vignette("yuima-integration", package = "dnsr").

library(dnsr)

The Nelson-Siegel Model

The Nelson-Siegel model is a parsimonious parametric model for the yield curve. It expresses the yield curve as a function of maturity using three factors:

y(m)=β1+β2(1−e−λmλm)+β3(1−e−λmλm−e−λm)y(m) = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \left(\frac{1-e^{-\lambda m}}{\lambda m}\right) + \beta_3 \left(\frac{1-e^{-\lambda m}}{\lambda m} - e^{-\lambda m}\right)

where:

  • y(m)y(m) is the yield at maturity mm
  • β1\beta_1 represents the long-term level of interest rates
  • β2\beta_2 represents the slope of the yield curve (short-term minus long-term rates)
  • β3\beta_3 represents the curvature or “hump” of the yield curve
  • λ\lambda controls the decay rate of the factor loadings

The model is popular because:

  1. It is flexible enough to capture various yield curve shapes
  2. It has a clear economic interpretation
  3. It is parsimonious, requiring only 4 parameters

Dynamic Extension

The DNS model extends the static Nelson-Siegel model by allowing the factors (β1\beta_1, β2\beta_2, β3\beta_3) to vary over time. These factors are modeled as stochastic processes, typically using Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes:

dβi(t)=κi(θi−βi(t))dt+σidWi(t)d\beta_i(t) = \kappa_i(\theta_i - \beta_i(t))dt + \sigma_i dW_i(t)

where:

  • κi\kappa_i is the speed of mean reversion
  • θi\theta_i is the long-run mean
  • σi\sigma_i is the volatility
  • Wi(t)W_i(t) is a Wiener process

This dynamic extension allows for modeling the time evolution of yield curves and scenario generation.

Getting Treasury Yield Data

The first step is to download Treasury yield curve data. The dnsr package provides functions to download and process this data:

# Set FRED API key first (do once per session)
Sys.setenv(fred_api_key = "your_api_key_here")

# Download recent Treasury yield curve data (last ~2 years)
yield_data <- get_treasury_yield_combined(start_date = "2022-01-01")

# Look at the data structure
head(yield_data)
# For this vignette, we'll create a small synthetic dataset
dates <- seq(as.Date("2023-01-01"), as.Date("2023-12-31"), by = "week")
maturities <- c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, 30)

# Create synthetic yield data frame
set.seed(123)
yield_data <- data.frame(Date = dates)

# Base yield curve shape
base_curve <- c(0.035, 0.037, 0.039, 0.040, 0.042, 0.043, 0.044, 0.045, 0.046, 0.045)

for (i in seq_along(maturities)) {
  # Add time series variation to each maturity
  m <- maturities[i]
  col_name <- as.character(m)
  
  # Create synthetic yields with level, slope, and curvature variations
  level_trend <- 0.005 * sin(2 * pi * (1:length(dates)) / length(dates))
  slope_effect <- 0.001 * (max(maturities) - m) * cos(4 * pi * (1:length(dates)) / length(dates))
  curvature_effect <- 0.001 * exp(-(m - 5)^2) * sin(6 * pi * (1:length(dates)) / length(dates))
  
  yield_data[[col_name]] <- base_curve[i] + level_trend + slope_effect + curvature_effect + 
    rnorm(length(dates), 0, 0.0005)
}

Fitting the DNS Model

Now that we have yield curve data, we can fit the DNS model:

# Fit the DNS model to historical yield curves
dns_result <- fit_dns_model(yield_data, show_progress = TRUE)

# Look at the fitted parameters
head(dns_result$parameters)

We can visualize the fitted yield curves to assess the model’s performance:

# Plot actual vs. fitted yield curves for a few dates
p <- plot_yield_curves(yield_data, dns_result)
p

We can also examine the time series of the fitted factors:

# Plot the factor time series
factor_plots <- plot_factor_time_series(dns_result)
factor_plots$factors

Estimating Factor Dynamics

To capture the dynamics of the yield curve, we need to estimate the stochastic processes governing the factors:

# Estimate factor dynamics
dynamics <- estimate_dns_dynamics(dns_result$parameters)

# Look at the estimated parameters
cat("Level factor (β₁):\n")
cat("  Mean reversion speed (κ):", round(dynamics$beta1$kappa, 4), "\n")
cat("  Long-run mean (θ):", round(dynamics$beta1$theta, 4), "\n")
cat("  Volatility (σ):", round(dynamics$beta1$sigma, 4), "\n")
cat("  Half-life:", round(dynamics$beta1$half_life_days, 1), "days\n\n")

cat("Slope factor (β₂):\n")
cat("  Mean reversion speed (κ):", round(dynamics$beta2$kappa, 4), "\n")
cat("  Long-run mean (θ):", round(dynamics$beta2$theta, 4), "\n")
cat("  Volatility (σ):", round(dynamics$beta2$sigma, 4), "\n")
cat("  Half-life:", round(dynamics$beta2$half_life_days, 1), "days\n\n")

cat("Curvature factor (β₃):\n")
cat("  Mean reversion speed (κ):", round(dynamics$beta3$kappa, 4), "\n")
cat("  Long-run mean (θ):", round(dynamics$beta3$theta, 4), "\n")
cat("  Volatility (σ):", round(dynamics$beta3$sigma, 4), "\n")
cat("  Half-life:", round(dynamics$beta3$half_life_days, 1), "days\n\n")

# Look at factor correlations
print(round(dynamics$correlation, 3))

The estimated dynamics give us insights into how the yield curve evolves over time. For example:

  • The level factor typically has slow mean reversion (long half-life)
  • The slope factor has moderate mean reversion
  • The curvature factor often has the fastest mean reversion

Simulating Future Yield Curves

We can use the estimated dynamics to simulate future yield curve scenarios. The package offers two simulation methods:

  1. Basic Simulation: Using standard discretization methods
  2. Advanced Simulation: Using the YUIMA package for accurate SDE simulation (covered in the YUIMA integration vignette)

Here we’ll demonstrate the basic simulation:

# Convert dynamics to simulation parameters
sim_params <- dns_dynamics_to_sim_params(dynamics)

# Get initial factors from most recent observation
initial_factors <- as.numeric(dns_result$parameters[1, c("beta1", "beta2", "beta3")])

# Simulate yield curves
sim_result <- simulate_dns_yield_curves(
  params = sim_params,
  initial_factors = initial_factors,
  maturities = as.numeric(names(yield_data)[-1]),
  time_horizon = 5,   # 5 years
  n_steps = 60,       # Monthly steps
  n_paths = 100       # 100 simulation paths
)

# Plot simulated yield curves at specific horizons
yield_plots <- plot_simulated_yields(
  sim_result, 
  time_points = c(0, 1, 3, 5),  # Now, 1 year, 3 years, 5 years
  path_subset = 1:5             # Show 5 paths
)

yield_plots$yield_curves

We can also examine the evolution of the simulated factors:

# Plot simulated factors
factor_sim_plots <- plot_simulated_factors(sim_result)
factor_sim_plots$level

Advanced Stochastic Simulation

For more advanced stochastic simulation using the YUIMA package, we can use the enhanced simulation functions:

# Check if YUIMA is installed
if (requireNamespace("yuima", quietly = TRUE)) {
  # Simulate using YUIMA's Euler-Maruyama scheme
  yuima_sim <- simulate_dns_yield_curves(
    params = sim_params,
    initial_factors = initial_factors,
    maturities = as.numeric(names(yield_data)[-1]),
    time_horizon = 5,
    n_steps = 60,
    n_paths = 100,
    sim_method = "euler"  # Use YUIMA's Euler-Maruyama scheme
  )
  
  # Plot the results
  yuima_plots <- plot_simulated_yields(
    yuima_sim, 
    time_points = c(0, 1, 3, 5)
  )
  
  # See the YUIMA integration vignette for more details on advanced simulation
}

Visualizing DNS Model Properties

The DNS model’s flexibility comes from its factor loadings structure. We can visualize these loadings:

# Plot factor loadings
p <- plot_dns_loadings(
  maturities = seq(0, 30, length.out = 100),
  lambda = dns_result$parameters$lambda[1]
)
p

Advanced Visualizations

The package provides several additional visualization functions:

Heat Map of Yield Curve Evolution 

# Create a heat map of yield curve evolution
p <- plot_yield_heatmap(yield_data)
p

3D Yield Surface 

# Create a 3D visualization (requires plotly)
if (requireNamespace("plotly", quietly = TRUE)) {
  surface <- plot_yield_surface(yield_data)
  # For non-interactive output:
  # plotly::orca(surface, "yield_surface.png")
}

PCA Analysis 

# Perform principal component analysis
pca_result <- plot_yield_pca(yield_data)
pca_result$plots$weights

Model Comparison

The DNS model can be compared to other term structure models:

# Compare DNS with other models for a specific date
comparison <- compare_term_structure_models(
  yield_data,
  date_to_compare = yield_data$Date[1],
  models = c("NS", "Spline")
)
comparison$plot

Conclusion

The dnsr package provides a comprehensive framework for yield curve modeling using the Dynamic Nelson-Siegel approach. It offers tools for:

  1. Downloading and preprocessing Treasury yield data
  2. Fitting the DNS model to historical data
  3. Estimating factor dynamics
  4. Simulating future yield curve scenarios
  5. Visualizing results in various formats

For advanced stochastic simulation using the YUIMA package, please refer to the dedicated vignette:

vignette("dnsr-yuima-integration", package = "dnsr")

These capabilities make it valuable for interest rate risk management, ALM modeling, economic scenario generation, and fixed income research.

For more details on specific functions, please refer to their documentation.
